readerTitle: Nobody picked this option. It still made the company money.
caseNote: 실제 연구 (Ariely 2008의 Economist 교실 실험, Huber et al. 1982, Frederick et al. 2014) + 가상 사례 (팝콘, 커피 사이즈)
insight: 사람들은 옵션을 하나씩 평가하지 않고, 가장 정당화하기 쉬운 것을 고른다.
misconception: 아무도 사지 않는 옵션은 없애야 한다. 디코이는 언제나 통한다.

sources.text: Ariely (2008). Predictably Irrational, Ch. 1 "The Truth about Relativity".
Huber, Payne & Puto (1982). Adding Asymmetrically Dominated Alternatives. J. of Consumer Research.
Frederick, Lee & Baskin (2014). The Limits of Attraction. J. of Marketing Research.

factChecks.note: Ariely의 Economist 실험은 MIT 학생 100명 대상의 교실 실험이며 『Predictably Irrational』(2008)에 실린 것입니다. 표본이 작다는 점을 "classroom experiment"로 표시했습니다.
재현성 논란(Frederick et al., 2014)을 6번 카드에 넣었습니다. "판단력 훈련"이라는 포지셔닝에는 효과의 한계를 같이 가르치는 것이 신뢰에 도움이 됩니다.
팝콘 가격은 설명을 위한 가상 수치이며, 카드에 그렇게 표기했습니다.

cards.title: Nobody picked this option. It still made the company money.
body: In a well-known classroom experiment, adding a choice that **zero people** picked changed what everyone else bought.

image.label: Three subscription cards, one faded
image.brief: 잡지 구독 가격 카드 3장이 나란히. 가운데 카드만 반투명하게 흐릿하게 처리. 실제 매체 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Which subscription would you choose?
body: A news magazine offers three one-year plans:

options.feedback: **16%** of the students in the experiment picked this.
**0%** picked this. Nobody at all. Hold that thought.
**84%** picked this. Print + Web looks like getting the web version for free.

choice.afterReveal: Most readers pick the same plan. Next: what happened when the option nobody chose was taken away.

cards.title: Then the option nobody wanted was removed.
body: Dan Ariely ran the offer past 100 MIT students. Then he showed another group only two options, at the same prices.
cards.callout: Revenue per 100 students: **$11,444** with the decoy, **$8,012** without. About 43% more, from an option nobody bought.

image.label: Then the option nobody wanted was removed.
image.brief: Labeled HTML chart from the lesson numbers

cards.title: The decoy effect
body: A **decoy** is an option that's clearly worse than one target option, but not clearly worse than the others.

Print only at $125 is obviously worse than Print + Web at $125. It's hard to compare with Web only at $59. The decoy makes one comparison effortless, so that option starts to look like the smart choice.
Researchers call this **asymmetric dominance**. Huber, Payne and Puto first showed it in 1982.

image.label: Target beats decoy; competitor is hard to compare
image.brief: 카드 3장 다이어그램. 타깃(Print+Web)이 디코이(Print)를 이기는 화살표 "같은 가격, 더 많이". 경쟁 옵션(Web)과는 물음표로 연결.

cards.title: The popcorn stand.
body: The medium is mostly there to make the large look like a bargain. For 50 cents more, why not?
Look for the same pattern in coffee sizes, phone storage tiers and software plans.

cards.title: Decoys are weaker than the famous story suggests.
body: Later research found the effect is smaller and less reliable in realistic settings. A 2014 paper by Frederick, Lee and Baskin had trouble reproducing it across many real product choices.
Decoys work best when people don't have strong preferences and the options are easy to compare on one or two numbers.
A decoy that looks obviously fake can make your whole pricing page feel manipulative.

cards.title: Your coffee shop sells two sizes.
body: Small is $3.00. Large is $4.50. You'd like more people to choose Large, which has the better margin.
You add a Medium. What should it cost?

options.feedback: This Medium is a good deal on its own. It will pull buyers from both sizes, mostly from Large.
That's the decoy. For 30 cents more, Large is clearly the better buy. Most people won't pick Medium, and that's the point.
A Medium that costs more than Large isn't a decoy. It's confusing, and customers will wonder what they're missing.

cards.title: Design the comparison, not just the price.
body: People rarely judge an option on its own. They pick the one that's easiest to justify.
**Try it today:** which plan on your pricing page do you most want people to choose? Is there something next to it that makes it easy to justify?
